summary: This informational document republishes PKCS #5 version 2.1 from RSA Laboratories. It gives recommendations for password-based cryptography, covering key derivation functions, encryption schemes, message authentication schemes and ASN.1 syntax identifying the techniques.

eli5.summary: A password is short, but a strong lock needs a long key. This explains how to turn a password into a good key safely.

questions: what is the difference between pbes1 and pbes2
how many pbkdf2 iterations should i use
subtitle: How to turn a short password into a strong key, and use it for encryption and message authentication.

tldr.problem: Passwords are short and guessable, but encryption and authentication need proper keys. An attacker can also try many passwords offline.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #5 combines the password with a salt and an iteration count in a key derivation function (PBKDF1 or PBKDF2). That key then drives an encryption scheme (PBES1, PBES2) or a message authentication scheme (PBMAC1).
tldr.outcome: PBKDF2, PBES2 and PBMAC1 are recommended for new applications; PBKDF1 and PBES1 are kept only for compatibility. The document obsoletes RFC 2898 and has since been updated.

today: RFC 8018 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2898. It is updated by RFC 9579 and RFC 9879.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 8018 gives recommendations for implementing password-based cryptography: key derivation functions, encryption schemes, message authentication schemes, and the ASN.1 syntax that identifies them. They are meant for general use and are particularly intended for protecting sensitive information such as private keys, as in PKCS #8.

It is a republication of PKCS #5 v2.1 from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards series and supersedes PKCS #5 version 2.0 (RFC 2898) while keeping compatible techniques. Password-based key establishment protocols and guidelines for choosing passwords are out of scope.
sections.eli5: It is a recipe book for turning a password into a secret key, used for protecting things like private keys.

sections.title: Salt and Iteration Count
sections.content:
Password-based key derivation here is a function of a password, a salt and an iteration count. The salt and count need not be kept secret.

A salt selects one key out of a large set derived from the password. With a 64-bit salt there can be as many as 2^64 keys per password, so an attacker cannot precompute keys for a dictionary of passwords. The RFC recommends a random salt of at least eight octets (64 bits). If different uses of the same key could interact, the salt should also contain data that distinguishes operations and key lengths, and the receiver should check or regenerate it.

The iteration count makes each key more expensive to compute. A count of c adds log2(c) bits of security strength against trial-based attacks. The RFC follows FIPS SP 800-132: as large as acceptable to users, with a minimum of 1,000 recommended and 10,000,000 possibly appropriate for especially critical keys or very powerful systems.
sections.eli5: The salt is a pinch of random seasoning so two people with the same password still get different keys. The iteration count is how many times you stir, to make guessing slow for a thief.

sections.title: Key Derivation: PBKDF1 and PBKDF2
sections.content:
PBKDF1 applies a hash function (MD2, MD5 or SHA-1) c times to the password joined with the salt. The derived key is limited by the hash output: 16 octets for MD2 and MD5, 20 octets for SHA-1. It is recommended only for compatibility with existing applications.

PBKDF2 uses a pseudorandom function (PRF). For each output block i, it computes U_1 = PRF(P, S || INT(i)), then U_2 = PRF(P, U_1) and so on up to U_c, and XORs the c results together. The blocks are concatenated and truncated to dkLen. The maximum key length is (2^32 - 1) * hLen, so it is essentially unbounded, and PBKDF2 is recommended for new applications.

The RFC calls the PBKDF2 construction 'belt-and-suspenders': the recursion removes a degree of parallelism from an opponent and the XOR reduces concerns about degenerating into a small set of values.
sections.eli5: PBKDF1 is the older, smaller blender. PBKDF2 is the newer one that can make a key of any length, by stirring the mixture many times.

sections.title: Encryption and Authentication Schemes
sections.content:
PBES1 combines PBKDF1 with DES or RC2 in CBC mode. It uses an eight-octet salt, derives 16 octets, and splits them into an eight-octet key and an eight-octet initialization vector. It is for compatibility only, since its key sizes (56 or 64 bits) may not be large enough.

PBES2 combines a password-based key derivation function (PBKDF2 in this version) with an underlying encryption scheme. The salt, iteration count, key length and algorithm identifiers can be conveyed to the decryptor in an AlgorithmIdentifier value. It is recommended for new applications. Appendix B lists AES-CBC-Pad among the example underlying schemes.

PBMAC1 does the same for authentication: PBKDF2 derives a key, and an underlying message authentication scheme such as HMAC with SHA-1 or the SHA-2 family produces the MAC. Verification outputs 'correct' or 'incorrect'.
sections.eli5: Once you have your strong key, you can lock a message with it (encryption) or stamp it so nobody can change it unnoticed (authentication).

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that password-based cryptography is limited in the security it can provide, especially because offline password search is possible. Salt and iteration count raise the attacker's cost, but it remains essential that passwords are selected well and protected if stored.

Different keys should be derived for different uses to minimize unintended interactions. A random salt is enough for password-based encryption with a single algorithm; other situations need a structured salt. The RFC also points to separate documents on security considerations for MD2, MD5 and SHA-1.
sections.eli5: Even a great recipe cannot save a very easy password. Pick a good one and keep it safe.
